courseMetadata.title: Testing Strategy for Senior Developers
courseMetadata.description: Decide **what** to test, **at which layer**, and **what to leave alone**. Take an app from ad hoc tests to a deliberate pyramid: unit tests that catch planted bugs, integration tests against a real database, a consumer-driven **contract test**, one or two stable e2e flows, and a written rationale you can defend. Hands-on throughout, with runnable JavaScript, Python and SQL.

prerequisites.description: Comfortable writing and running automated tests in at least one language (e.g. Jest, pytest, JUnit).
Working knowledge of JavaScript and basic Python and SQL, enough to read and edit short programs.
Experience with a web app that has a frontend, an HTTP API and a database; your own app can serve as the course project.

competencies.title: Choosing the right test layer
competencies.description: Given a behaviour or change, decide whether it belongs at the unit, integration, contract or e2e layer, weighing risk, feedback speed, cost, and where the logic actually lives.

desiredOutcomes.description: Apply the testing pyramid to decide what to **unit** test vs **integration** test vs **e2e** test.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Correct layer with a where-the-logic-lives justification in novel scenarios.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The pyramid is a fixed ratio, like 70% unit, 20% integration, 10% e2e.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The shape comes from cost and speed trade-offs applied to where an app's logic lives. A thin data service can correctly be integration-heavy; a ratio target produces filler tests and deletes useful ones.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run worked example s1-we-1 and the thin-service question: derive the shape from twelve 'cheapest test that would fail' answers rather than from a picture.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Higher-layer tests are more realistic, so they're always better.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Realism costs speed, stability and failure localisation. The library's 140 green browser tests missed a fee bug that one unit test would have caught.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Revisit the Section 1 opening story and the flow table in s3-we-1, where the most expensive risk is deliberately tested below e2e.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Every line of code needs a test.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Testing effort should follow risk and the cost of failure. Some behaviours are rightly left untested with a stated reason and revisit trigger.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Study rows 10–12 of the s1-we-1 risk map and the 'deliberately untested' part of the s3-we-4 rationale.

competencies.title: Unit testing business logic
competencies.description: Write fast, deterministic unit tests for domain rules that assert on behaviour rather than implementation and cover boundaries and edge cases.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write unit tests for business rules that catch at least 80% of planted bugs (mutants).
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Boundary tests that kill named mutants.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A unit is a class or a function, so each class gets its own test file and each method its own test.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A unit is a unit of behaviour tested through a public entry point. Class-shaped tests break whenever internals are reorganised, even when behaviour is unchanged.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-read the three habits in s1-exp-unit-tests and rewrite one class-shaped test as a rule-shaped test.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If my tests pass, they're good tests.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A test that also passes against obviously wrong code checks nothing. Mutation testing shows whether a test can fail; boundary inputs are usually what make it able to.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run s1-run-2 (weak vs strong test) and repeat worked example s1-we-2 against the four mutants.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Testing private methods directly improves coverage quality.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It couples tests to implementation details. If a private helper matters, some public behaviour depends on it; test that behaviour.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Revisit the cap-constant question in the Section 1 quiz and find the public behaviour a private helper supports.

competencies.title: Test doubles and designing for testability
competencies.description: Choose between stubs, fakes, mocks and real dependencies, and introduce seams (dependency injection, ports and adapters) so logic can be isolated.

desiredOutcomes.description: Refactor hard-to-test code by adding a seam and test it with fakes that assert on outcomes.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Correct double per dependency; outcome assertions; knows where fakes belong at each layer.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Everything that isn't the unit under test should be mocked.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Over-mocking verifies wiring, not behaviour, and breaks on harmless refactors. At the integration layer, faking your own database or modules removes exactly what the layer is for.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Replay worked example s1-we-3's batching refactor and the s2 dependency table (s2-we-3).

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Mocks and fakes are basically the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Mocks assert on how they were called; fakes provide small working behaviour you inspect afterwards. Choosing the wrong one makes tests brittle or blind.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Use the stub/fake/mock table in s1-exp-seams to classify each double in one of your own tests.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Hard-to-test code just needs cleverer tests: patch the globals, intercept the imports.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Difficulty testing is a design signal. Passing dependencies in (a seam) makes the code testable with plain objects and improves the design.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the seam challenge in s1-exp-seams, starting from the 'before' notifier.

competencies.title: Integration testing the API layer
competencies.description: Test HTTP handlers together with real persistence and real serialisation, keeping tests isolated, repeatable and reasonably fast.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write isolated integration tests for an API against a real database and predict the stored state after requests.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Fresh state per test; asserts on stored rows as well as responses.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An in-memory mock of the database is good enough for API tests.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Mocked persistence hides query, constraint, NULL, transaction and migration bugs, which are exactly what integration tests exist to catch. Fakes can even be stricter than the real database.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run the two predict-then-run programs in s2-exp-integration (NULL count; fake vs UNIQUE) and the seed-rollback twist in s2-we-2.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Integration tests should share one seeded database.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Shared mutable state makes results depend on test order and turns parallel runs into random failures. Each test needs its own known state.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-read the isolation step of s2-we-1 and rebuild your suite with a fresh database per test.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Integration tests are just slow unit tests.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: They target a different defect class (wiring, configuration, persistence and boundary behaviour), not business-rule combinations.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Compare the defect list in s2-exp-integration with the Section 1 unit examples, and move rule-combination checks down.

competencies.title: Consumer-driven contract testing
competencies.description: Write a contract test that captures what the frontend expects from the backend and verify the provider against it, catching schema or shape mismatches before deployment.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write a **contract test** that catches a frontend/backend mismatch.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Consumer-owned, minimal contract verified in the provider's build.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Once we have contract tests, we don't need integration or e2e tests.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Contracts check the agreed shape of messages, not business correctness. A double booking has a perfectly valid shape.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Study the defect comparison table in s2-exp-contracts.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Our OpenAPI spec is our contract test.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A spec is documentation unless something automatically checks both the consumer's real usage and the provider's real responses against it. A spec regenerated from the backend happily documents a breaking rename.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Revisit the rename story and s2-we-4; identify which build fails in each approach.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The provider team should define the contract, listing everything the API returns.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Consumer-driven contracts list only what consumers use, so harmless additions don't break builds and real dependencies are explicit.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the verifyContract challenge and check the extra-field case.

competencies.title: Targeted end-to-end testing
competencies.description: Pick the one or two user flows whose failure is most costly and write stable e2e tests for them, using resilient selectors, controlled data and deliberate waits.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write one or two stable e2e tests for critical flows and fix flaky tests at their root.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Flows chosen by the three conditions; root-cause flakiness fixes without retries.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More e2e tests mean more confidence.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Past the critical flows, each extra browser test adds minutes and flakiness faster than signal; the detail it checks is caught faster and more precisely lower down.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-read the 400-test story and the three conditions in s3-exp-e2e-flakiness.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Flaky tests are a retry problem.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Flakiness has causes (timing, shared state, non-determinism, environment). Retries hide them, including real product bugs.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Work through s3-we-2's diagnosis and the flakiness root-cause table.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: E2e tests should check every field and edge case.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Detail belongs in unit and contract tests; e2e confirms the flow works as a whole with one outcome assertion.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Compare the brittle and stable Playwright examples in s3-exp-e2e-flakiness.

competencies.title: Evaluating an existing test suite
competencies.description: Audit a suite for gaps (untested high-risk behaviour) and over-investment (redundant, brittle or slow tests at the wrong layer) using coverage data, mutation testing, runtime profiles and a risk map.

desiredOutcomes.description: **Evaluate** an existing test suite for gaps or over-investment.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Uses all four lenses; at least three gaps and three over-investments with evidence.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: High line coverage means the code is well tested.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Coverage records what ran, not what was checked. A smoke test with no assertions can give 100% line coverage; mutation score measures checking.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run s3-run-2 and redo the mutationScore challenge.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Deleting tests is always risky.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Redundant, slow or brittle tests cost runtime and upkeep every day. Removing them after checking what they cover is maintenance.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Revisit the judgment step of s3-we-3 and the fix-the-audit challenge.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Gaps are found by looking at uncovered files in the coverage report.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The dangerous gaps are high-risk behaviours with weak or missing assertions, often in 'covered' code. Start from the risk map.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-read the gap step of s3-we-3: none of its three gaps showed up as uncovered lines.

competencies.title: Articulating a test strategy
competencies.description: Write a short, defensible rationale explaining layer choices, what was deliberately left untested, the accepted risk, and what would change the decision.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write a short rationale for what was left untested and why.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Context, layers, deliberately untested with accepted risk, revisit triggers.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Leaving something untested is an admission of failure.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A reasoned omission with an accepted risk and a revisit trigger is a strategic choice. The real problem is untested code with no explanation.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the faded variant in s3-we-4 and write three 'deliberately untested' entries for your project.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A test strategy is a coverage target.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A target is an output. A strategy explains where effort goes and why, which a coverage number can't.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Compare the ticketing rationale excerpt with a one-line coverage target and list what the target omits.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- A layer decision is made behaviour by behaviour, by asking **what is the cheapest test that would fail if this broke?**
- The pyramid shape is a *consequence* of those answers, not a quota. Thin data services can be integration-heavy, and that's correct.
- A test is only valuable if it **fails when the code is wrong**. Mutation testing measures exactly that.
- A unit is a unit of **behaviour**, tested through public entry points.
- Hard-to-test code is a design signal: add a **seam**, then prefer stubs and fakes that assert on outcomes over mocks that assert on calls.
keyTakeaways: Choose the **lowest layer that can see the bug**.
Shape follows risk; never aim for a ratio.
Test boundaries: the last good value and the first bad one.
Green isn't proof: run your tests against a mutant.
Pass dependencies in; test with fakes; assert on outcomes.

learningExperiences.title: The layer decision: risk maps and the pyramid

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

A city library launched a new lending system. Two weeks later a retired patron complained: she returned a DVD 20 days late and was charged **$8.00**. Seniors pay half, so the charge should have been **$4.00**.

The team had 140 automated tests, all green. Most drove a browser through the checkout screen. None checked a senior returning a DVD late enough to hit the fee cap. That combination lived deep inside one small function, and no browser test was ever going to enumerate it.

The lesson is not "write more tests". It is that **the test for this bug belonged at a different layer**. This section is about choosing that layer on purpose.

## In this section you will

- Produce a **risk map** of an app, ranking behaviours by likelihood and cost of failure.
- Assign 10 or more behaviours to a **test layer**, each with a one-sentence justification.
- Write unit tests that catch at least **80% of planted bugs** (mutants).
- Add a **seam** to hard-to-test code and test it with a **fake** rather than a mock.

The code exercises run in the browser. JavaScript always works offline; the **first** Python or SQL run needs a network connection because those runtimes download once and are then cached.

## Key terms

- **Test layer**: how much of the system a test runs at once. This course uses four:
- **Unit test**: one piece of behaviour, in memory, in milliseconds. *"A senior's capped DVD fee is halved."*
- **Integration test**: your code plus real infrastructure such as a database. *"POST /loans stores a row with the right due date."* (Section 2)
- **Contract test**: checks that a separately deployed frontend and backend agree on message shape. (Section 2)
- **End-to-end (e2e) test**: drives the whole deployed system as a user would, usually through a browser. (Section 3)
- **Testing pyramid**: lower layers are cheaper, faster and better at pinpointing failures, so *usually* most tests belong low down. The shape is a result of trade-offs, not a rule.
- **Risk**: likelihood that something breaks × cost when it does.

## The layer decision: four questions

For every behaviour, ask:

1. **Where does the logic live?** Pure calculation lives in your code, so a unit test can see it. Logic in a SQL query, a database constraint, framework configuration or the boundary between two apps can only be seen by a test that includes that thing.
2. **What does a failure cost?** Money, safety, legal exposure and lost users are expensive. A misaligned icon is cheap.
3. **How likely is it to break?** Many branches, frequent change, tricky arithmetic, time zones, several people touching it.
4. **What is the cheapest test that would fail if this broke?** This is the deciding question. Choose **the lowest layer that can see the bug**.

The pyramid shape falls out of these answers. In most apps, most risky logic is calculation and decision-making, so most tests land at the unit layer. A thin service that mostly moves data between an API and a database has its risk in queries and wiring, so its suite will be integration-heavy, and that is correct. Some teams call that shape a "trophy" or "honeycomb"; the name matters less than the reason.

## An analogy: inspecting a building

You don't check whether every brick is sound by walking through the finished building and tapping walls. You test bricks at the factory (unit), check that the plumbing connects to the mains (integration), confirm the electrician's plugs fit the builder's sockets (contract), and do one final walkthrough before handing over the keys (e2e). The walkthrough matters, but it's the worst place to discover a bad brick.

## Watch out: the ratio trap

The most common misreading of the pyramid is **"we need 70% unit, 20% integration, 10% e2e"** (misconception `mc-pyramid-fixed-ratio`). Teams that chase a ratio write filler unit tests for code that has no logic, and delete integration tests that were guarding real query bugs. The close cousin is **"higher layers are more realistic, so they're better"** (`mc-higher-layer-always-better`): the library's 140 browser tests were very realistic and missed the bug completely.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before reading the worked example: pick **one** behaviour of the library system (late fees, renewals, checkout, login, search...) and predict the layer you would test it at. Write one sentence saying why.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your sentence with the question *what is the cheapest test that would fail if this broke?* If your reason was "it's the most realistic" or "we need more unit tests", you were reasoning from realism or a ratio, not from where the logic lives. The worked example below applies the four questions to twelve behaviours.

interactionSequence.prompt: Order these four test layers from **fastest, most precise feedback** (first) to **slowest, least precise** (last).
options: End-to-end browser test
Unit test
Contract test
Integration test against a real database

optionFeedback.feedback: Slowest and least precise: a failure could come from any part of the whole system.
Fastest: runs in memory in milliseconds and points at one rule.
Runs a handler and checks message shape; seconds, and points at a specific field.
Seconds, because it starts a real database, but still points at a specific query or constraint.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Unit → integration → contract → e2e is the usual order for speed and failure localisation. Contract and integration tests are both in the middle and can swap depending on setup; what matters is that e2e is the most expensive place to learn about a bug, which is why it holds the fewest tests.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your ordering?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team's service mostly receives form data, validates required fields and writes rows to a database; there is little calculation. Their suite is 60% integration tests. A new lead says the pyramid requires 70% unit tests. What is the best response?
options: Rewrite integration tests as unit tests until the ratio is 70/20/10.
Keep the integration-heavy shape, because the risk lives in queries and wiring that only integration tests can see.
Replace most tests with e2e tests, since they are the most realistic.
Add a unit test for every function to reach the ratio without deleting anything.

optionFeedback.feedback: The ratio isn't a rule. Rewriting would move tests away from where this app's bugs live.
Right. The shape follows where the logic lives, and in a thin data service that's the database boundary.
Realism costs speed and failure localisation, and e2e adds nothing here that integration misses.
Tests written to hit a count, not a risk, cost upkeep and catch little.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Run the four questions: *where does the logic live?* Mostly in SQL and constraints. *What's the cheapest test that would fail?* One that includes the real database. So an integration-heavy suite is the correct result of the reasoning. Aiming for 70/20/10 would be reasoning backwards from a picture.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer names the low impact (a slightly worse ranking annoys but costs little), the fact that it's judged by eye, and the **revisit trigger** (complaints appear). Forgetting leaves no reason and no trigger; a decision records both, so it can be challenged later. Section 3 turns this into the *deliberately untested* part of a strategy rationale.

workedExamples.title: Risk-mapping the library system
workedExamples.problem: The library's lending system has twelve behaviours worth considering. Decide, for each, which layer should test it, or whether to leave it deliberately untested.
steps: **List behaviours, not files.** Write what the system *does*, in words a librarian would use: "late fee calculation", "renewal rules", "kiosk checkout", not `FeeService.ts`.
**Score each behaviour.** Likelihood 1–3 × impact 1–3. Late fees score 9: many rules, change every budget year, and they involve money. The monthly report scores 1.

**Find where the logic lives.** Late fees, renewals, barcodes and hold ordering are pure functions. The checkout API's due date lives partly in SQL and the schema. The due date on the patron app depends on a field name agreed between two teams.

learningExperiences.title: Unit tests that can actually fail

contentBlocks.content:
## Three habits of tests that can fail

A unit test is only worth having if **it would fail when the behaviour is wrong**.

- **Test a behaviour, not a class.** A *unit* is one rule the business cares about, such as "child cards pay no fees", tested through its public entry point. If one rule spans three small functions, test the rule; you can then reorganise the three functions without touching the tests.
- **Test at the edges.** Bugs cluster at boundaries: the first day late, the day the fee reaches its cap, the day after. Split inputs into groups that should behave the same (**equivalence classes**) and test the edges of each group.
- **Keep money in whole cents.** Fractions like `0.1` aren't exact in binary, so exact assertions on them break. Integer cents make exact assertions safe.

## Mutants: measuring whether a test can fail

- **Mutant**: a copy of your code with one small deliberate bug, such as `<=` changed to `<` or `500` changed to `5000`.
- **Mutation testing**: running your tests against many mutants. If a test fails, the mutant is **killed**. If every test still passes, it **survived**: your tests didn't notice the bug.
- **Equivalent mutant**: a change that can't alter behaviour for any input, so no test can kill it. You note it and move on.

Run the fee rule below, then compare a weak test with a strong one.

contentBlocks.title: Why `0.1 * 3 !== 0.3`
contentBlocks.content: Decimal fractions like 0.1 have no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one. `0.1 * 3` produces the nearest double, `0.30000000000000004`, so strict equality fails. Store fees in **whole cents** so tests like `expect(fee).toBe(30)` are exact, or use `toBeCloseTo` when a value really is fractional.

## About the code runner

The JavaScript test runner in this course is a **Jest-compatible subset, not Jest itself**: `describe`/`it`/`expect`, the common matchers, `beforeEach`/`afterEach` and `jest.fn` work, but there is **no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers**. Python exercises use the standard library's `unittest`. The limit happens to match the lesson: without module mocking, the only way to control a dependency is to design a seam for it.

## Common errors: unit tests

- **Trusting green.** A test that passes against the correct code *and* against obviously wrong code checks nothing. Run it against a mutant. (`mc-passing-test-is-good-test`)
- **One test file per class, one test per method.** Split the class and every test moves or breaks. Test rules, not structure. (`mc-unit-equals-class`)
- **Exporting private helpers to test them.** If a helper matters, some public behaviour depends on it, so test that. (`mc-test-private-methods`)
- **Only small inputs.** A suite that never exceeds the cap can't tell a cap of 500 from 5000.
- **Asserting `0.1 * 3 === 0.3`.** Use integer cents, or `toBeCloseTo` for real fractions.

Integer arithmetic (`10 * 3 === 30`) has no such problem. This is why fee logic stores whole cents: a test for the rule should fail only when the *rule* is wrong, not because of representation noise.

learningExperiences.title: Seams and test doubles: making hard code testable

contentBlocks.content:
## Test doubles and seams

- **Test double**: anything that stands in for a real dependency in a test.
- **Stub**: returns canned answers ("today is day 11").
- **Fake**: a small working implementation, such as an in-memory outbox that records emails.
- **Mock**: records how it was called, and the test asserts on those calls ("`send` was called once with these arguments").
- **Seam**: a place where you can swap a dependency without editing the code under test, typically by passing it in as a parameter (dependency injection).

Some code is hard to unit test because it grabs its dependencies itself: it reads the system clock, imports an email client, or opens a database connection. The tempting fix is a clever trick such as patching globals. The better fix is to **change the design so the dependency is passed in**.

rows: What the code produces, given some input from a dependency
What ends up in the world after the code runs
an in-memory outbox you inspect afterwards
That a specific call happened, *and the call itself is the behaviour* (e.g. charge a card exactly once)

contentBlocks.title: Common errors (Section 1)
contentBlocks.content:
- **Aiming for a ratio.** Decide behaviour by behaviour and let the shape follow. (`mc-pyramid-fixed-ratio`)
- **Testing a rule through the browser because it feels real.** The senior-DVD bug sat behind 140 green browser tests. (`mc-higher-layer-always-better`)
- **Testing every line.** Effort should follow risk. (`mc-test-every-line`)
- **One test per class or method.** Test rules, not structure. (`mc-unit-equals-class`)
- **Trusting green.** Run tests against a mutant. (`mc-passing-test-is-good-test`)
- **Exporting private helpers to test them.** (`mc-test-private-methods`)
- **Mocking every collaborator.** You end up testing wiring. (`mc-mock-everything`, `mc-mocks-fakes-interchangeable`)
- **Patching globals instead of adding a seam.** If a test needs three tricks, change the code. (`mc-clever-tests-fix-hard-code`)

## Watch out: tricks instead of seams

If testing a module needs you to intercept `require`, freeze the system clock and block real emails, you're facing `mc-clever-tests-fix-hard-code`: the belief that hard-to-test code just needs cleverer tests. The difficulty is **information about the design**. Passing the clock and mailer in fixes the test *and* makes the code easier to reuse and reason about.

class FakeMailer:
    def __init__(self, sent=[]):
        self.sent = sent
    def send(self, to):
        self.sent.append(to)

a = FakeMailer()
a.send("ana@lib.org")
b = FakeMailer()
b.send("ben@lib.org")

## What you should now believe

- Integration tests target a **different defect class** from unit tests: queries, constraints, transactions, serialisation and configuration.
- At this layer the database stays **real**, and every test gets its own isolated state.
- Predict **both** the response and the stored rows; they can disagree.
- Fake only at the **outer edge**: systems you don't own that cost money or have side effects.
- Contract tests check **shape**; integration tests check **behaviour**. Neither replaces the other.

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

On a Monday morning, a vet clinic's booking page shows **"Invalid Date"** on every confirmation screen, and receptionists start phoning owners to confirm times by hand. On Friday, a backend developer had renamed the response field `startsAt` to `start_time`. The backend's tests were updated and passed. The frontend's tests used a hand-written JSON sample that still said `startsAt`, and they passed too.

Each side was tested; **the agreement between them was not**. This section builds the two layers that sit in that gap: **integration tests** for the API and its database, and **contract tests** for the frontend/backend boundary. It builds directly on Section 1's risk map, which put "the API stores the right row" at the integration layer and "the app shows the API's date" at the contract layer.

## In this section you will

- Write **isolated, repeatable integration tests** for API endpoints against a real database.
- **Predict** the stored rows and the response after a request, then verify with a test.
- Decide, dependency by dependency, whether to use the **real thing, a fake or a stub**.
- Write a **consumer-driven contract** test that fails on a planted rename or type change.
- Explain what contract tests catch that integration tests miss, and the reverse.

The Python and SQL exercises run in your browser; the **first** run needs a network connection while those runtimes download, and after that they're cached.

## Key terms

- **Integration test**: your code running with real infrastructure: the actual database engine, real SQL, the real schema and migrations, real serialisation.
- **Real persistence**: a genuine database engine rather than a dictionary pretending to be one. In CI this is usually a containerised copy of the production database (e.g. Postgres via Testcontainers). In this course it's in-memory **SQLite**: a real SQL engine whose dialect differs from Postgres in places.
- **Test isolation**: each test starts from a known state and leaves nothing behind, using a fresh schema, a rolled-back transaction, truncation or unique data per test.
- **Consumer** / **provider**: the side that *uses* an API / the side that *serves* it.
- **Contract**: a machine-checkable statement of the requests a consumer sends and the response fields and types it relies on.
- **Consumer-driven contract**: the consumer writes the contract, listing only what it uses; the provider proves in its own build that it honours it (**provider verification**).
- **Schema drift**: the two sides' idea of the message shape slowly diverging.

## What integration tests are for

Integration tests are not slow unit tests. They catch a **different class of defect**, the kind that lives *between* your code and its infrastructure:

- a query with a wrong `JOIN`, a missing `WHERE`, or surprising `NULL` handling
- a constraint (`UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, foreign key) missing from a migration, or doing work your code relies on
- transactions: what gets committed, what gets rolled back, and when
- serialisation: field names, date formats, how `null` comes out
- configuration: connection settings, routing, middleware order

A dictionary-based fake has none of these properties, so a test that uses one can't catch these bugs. **Speed is still a goal**: create the schema once, isolate each test cheaply, and leave business-rule combinations to unit tests (Section 1).

## Common errors: integration tests

- **Faking the database in API tests.** Constraint, query and transaction bugs pass silently. (`mc-mocked-db-good-enough`)
- **One shared seeded database for the whole suite.** Test B passes only if test A ran first; parallel runs turn that into random failures. (`mc-shared-seeded-db`)
- **Covering business-rule combinations with integration tests.** Slow, and duplicates the unit layer. (`mc-integration-is-slow-unit`)
- **Asserting only on the HTTP response.** A handler can return 201 without saving anything; check the stored rows.
- **Uncommitted seed data.** A rollback in the code under test can silently remove it (worked example s2-we-2).

workedExamples.problem: Write integration tests for `book_appointment` (above) that would catch a migration dropping the `UNIQUE` constraint.
steps: **Isolation first.** `setUp` builds a new in-memory database for each test; `tearDown` closes it. No test can see another's rows.

**Act through the handler; assert on the response AND the stored state.** A handler can return 201 without saving anything.

```python
import unittest

class BookAppointmentIntegration(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.db = connect()      # a brand-new real database for every test

    def tearDown(self):
        self.db.close()

    def test_valid_booking_is_stored(self):
        status, body = book_appointment(
            self.db, {"vet_id": 7, "pet_name": "Biscuit", "starts_at": "2026-10-01T09:00"})
        self.assertEqual(status, 201)
        row = self.db.execute(
            "SELECT vet_id, pet_name, starts_at FROM appointments WHERE id = ?", (body["id"],)).fetchone()
        self.assertEqual(row, (7, "Biscuit", "2026-10-01T09:00"))

    def test_double_booking_is_rejected_and_not_stored(self):
        slot = {"vet_id": 7, "starts_at": "2026-10-01T09:00"}
        book_appointment(self.db, {**slot, "pet_name": "Biscuit"})
        status, _ = book_appointment(self.db, {**slot, "pet_name": "Mochi"})
        self.assertEqual(status, 409)
        count = self.db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM appointments").fetchone()[0]
        self.assertEqual(count, 1)
```

  no UNIQUE constraint: 1/2 passed
  conflict returns 500: 1/2 passed
  validation removed: 2/2 passed
  snake_case response: 2/2 passed
  status not set: 2/2 passed
killed 2/5

    {"vet_id": 7, "pet_name": "Mochi", "starts_at": "2026-10-01T09:00"},
    {"vet_id": 8, "pet_name": "Mochi", "starts_at": "2026-10-01T09:00"},

409
201
400
(1, 7, 'Biscuit', 'booked')
(2, 8, 'Mochi', 'booked')

**The twist.** Remove the `with db:` around the seed insert so it's never committed. The run prints the same three statuses, but only one row: `(1, 8, 'Mochi', 'booked')`. **Biscuit is gone.**

**Explain it.** Python's `sqlite3`, in its default mode, opens a transaction implicitly on the first insert. The seed was still in that open transaction when request 1 hit the constraint, and the handler's `with db:` rolled the whole transaction back.
workedExamples.conclusion: Always predict **both the response and the stored state**; they can disagree. The twist is a real production pattern: a handler sharing a connection with uncommitted work can roll it back. A dictionary fake would print two rows and hide it. The isolation rule: **commit seed data explicitly**, or own each test's transaction and roll it back yourself.

## Two halves, two builds

1. **Consumer side (frontend build).** The frontend team writes a contract, e.g. "for `POST /appointments` I need `id` (number), `startsAt` (string) and `petName` (string)", with an example response. The frontend's own tests use a stub **generated from that contract**, instead of hand-written sample JSON that can drift.
2. **Provider side (backend build).** The backend runs its real handler and checks the response against every consumer's contract. If a field any consumer relies on is missing or has changed type, the **backend** build fails before deployment.

In industry, **Pact** is the common tool (with a broker that stores contracts between builds); Spring Cloud Contract fills the same role in Java. An **OpenAPI spec** is useful documentation, and only becomes a contract *test* when something automatically checks both the consumer's usage and the provider's responses against it.

## Common errors: contract tests

- **A contract that mirrors the provider's full response.** Every harmless new field breaks the build, and people start ignoring it. List only what the consumer uses. (`mc-provider-defines-contract`)
- **Calling an OpenAPI file "our contract tests".** Unless both sides are checked against it automatically, it's documentation. (`mc-openapi-is-contract-test`)
- **Deleting integration tests once contracts exist.** Contracts can't see business rules. (`mc-contract-replaces-integration`)
- **Running provider verification only in the frontend's build.** It must run where the provider's changes are made.

## Watch out: who owns the contract?

It feels natural for the team that builds the API to define it (`mc-provider-defines-contract`). But a provider-written schema lists everything the provider sends, not what anyone *uses*, so it fails on harmless additions and says nothing about which fields actually matter. Consumer-driven contracts invert this: each consumer states its real dependencies, and the provider is free to change anything no one relies on.

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

A ticketing company's web team has **400 browser tests**. A full run takes 55 minutes. About 6% of runs fail for no reason anyone can find, so CI retries each failure twice, and developers have stopped reading red builds; they just press "re-run".

In the same quarter, a bug let **two buyers purchase the same seat** for a sold-out show. None of the 400 tests tried two buyers at once. The team had invested heavily in the top of the pyramid and still missed its most expensive risk.

This section is about the top layer done small and well, then stepping back to judge a whole suite. It reuses Section 1's risk map and seams, and Section 2's isolation rule.

## In this section you will

- Choose **one or two** critical flows and write stable e2e tests for them.
- Fix a flaky test at its **root cause**, without retries.
- **Audit** a suite for at least three gaps and three over-investments, using coverage, mutation score and runtime data.
- Audit **your own** suite and act on it.
- Write a **strategy rationale** of one page or less.

## Key terms

- **Critical flow**: a user journey whose failure costs the most and that depends on many parts working together (buying a ticket, getting into the venue).
- **Flaky test**: sometimes passes, sometimes fails, **with no code change**.
- **Resilient selector**: finds an element the way a user would (its role and name, or its label), so it survives redesigns. Contrast `div:nth-child(3) > button`.
- **Controlled test data**: data each test creates for itself, so no other test can change it.
- **Line coverage** / **branch coverage**: the share of lines / branch sides that ran during tests.
- **Mutation score**: the share of non-equivalent mutants your tests kill.
- **Redundant test**: catches nothing another cheaper test doesn't already catch.
- **Test-suite audit**: a structured review for **gaps** (important risks with no test that would fail) and **over-investment** (tests costing more than they return).
- **Strategy rationale**: a short document explaining where testing effort goes and why, including what is deliberately untested.

## Choosing the one or two flows

Start from the risk map. A flow earns an e2e test only if **all three** are true:

1. **Its failure is among the most expensive** in the product.
2. **It crosses many parts**: frontend, several services, payment, email.
3. **Lower layers can't see it failing as a whole.** Each part may be unit and integration tested, but nothing else checks that they work *together*.

## Watch out: "more e2e, more confidence"

`mc-more-e2e-more-confidence` feels safe because e2e tests look like real use. Past the one or two critical flows, each extra browser test adds minutes and a new chance to flake, while the detail it checks would be caught faster and more precisely lower down. Its partner is `mc-flaky-fix-is-retry`: once the suite is too big to debug, retries become the default, and real product bugs start hiding behind them.

contentBlocks.content:
## Four lenses for an audit

Each lens alone misleads, so you need all four.

1. **Risk map vs tests (gaps).** For each high-risk behaviour, is there a test that *would fail* if it broke? Start from the risk map, not the coverage report: code can be covered without anything checking its result.
2. **Mutation score (checking strength).** Coverage says what ran; mutation score says what was *checked*. High coverage with a low mutation score means tests execute code without asserting much.
3. **Runtime and flakiness (cost).** Which tests take the most time? Which failed in reruns with no code change?
4. **Layer placement (over-investment).** Is any test checking detail at a higher layer than necessary, or duplicating what a cheaper test already catches?

contentBlocks.caption: A mutation score summary. Expected: `mutation score: 60%` and `look at: M3, M4`.
Both 'tests' execute every line (100% line coverage). Only the one that checks results catches the wrong member discount. Expected: `true`, `false`, `true`, `true`.

The ticketing suite's audit profile, computed by the (fixed) audit function. Mutants: M1 tier price wrong, M2 balcony/floor swapped, M3 VIP tier missing, M4 member discount wrong, M5 service fee skipped.

contentBlocks.altText: Chart: horizontal bars of runtime per test on a log scale. Two e2e tests at 9.4 s and 8.8 s dominate; the unit tests are a few milliseconds; the API test is 180 ms. The checkout e2e bar has a warning icon for 'failed once in 50 reruns'; three bars (api price endpoint, e2e price shown on page, unit renders logo) are outlined as 'redundancy candidates'.

contentBlocks.content:
## Writing the rationale

A strategy rationale answers four questions in one page or less:

1. **Context**: what the app does and where its risk lives.
2. **Layer choices**: what each layer covers, and why that layer.
3. **Deliberately untested**: each item, why, and the risk accepted.
4. **Revisit triggers**: the events that would change a decision.

It does not state a coverage number. A target is an output; a strategy explains the reasoning behind where effort goes.

contentBlocks.title: Rationale excerpt: ticketing platform
contentBlocks.content:
**Context.** Revenue depends on checkout and on entry at the door. The costliest failures are double-selling a seat and charging the wrong amount. Most logic is pricing and hold rules (pure code); the rest is persistence and a payment integration.

**Layers.** *Unit:* pricing, fees and seat-hold rules with an injected clock, about 70% of tests because that's where the logic is. *Integration:* every endpoint against Postgres in a container, including the `UNIQUE (event_id, seat_id)` ticket constraint. *Contract:* seat-map and checkout endpoints consumed by the web and door-scanner apps. *E2E:* exactly two flows, buying a ticket and scanning at the door.

**Deliberately untested.** Seat-map visual layout: checked by eye before each release; a bug is cheap and fixed within hours. The payment provider's fraud checks: their responsibility, and our adapter is contract-tested against their sandbox. The admin reports page: five internal users; a bug is annoying, not costly.

**Revisit if** a seat-map bug causes wrong purchases (add visual regression tests); reports start driving artist payouts (add integration tests); or e2e runtime exceeds 5 minutes or any e2e test fails in reruns (fix or remove before adding more).

contentBlocks.title: Common errors (Section 3)
contentBlocks.content:
- **Adding e2e tests to increase confidence.** Past the critical flows they add minutes and flakiness. (`mc-more-e2e-more-confidence`)
- **Automatic retries.** They hide timing, shared-state and clock bugs, including real product bugs. (`mc-flaky-fix-is-retry`)
- **Checking every field in a browser test.** Move detail down; assert the outcome. (`mc-e2e-checks-everything`)
- **Reading 90% coverage as well tested.** (`mc-high-coverage-well-tested`)
- **Refusing to delete any test.** Redundant tests cost runtime and upkeep daily. (`mc-deleting-tests-risky`)
- **Hunting gaps in the coverage report's red files.** Dangerous gaps are high-risk behaviours with weak assertions, even in covered code. (`mc-gaps-are-uncovered-files`)
- **Writing 'target: 90% coverage' as the strategy.** (`mc-strategy-is-coverage-target`)
- **Hiding untested areas** instead of listing them with reasons. (`mc-untested-is-failure`)

## Watch out: the coverage mirage

`mc-high-coverage-well-tested` and `mc-gaps-are-uncovered-files` usually travel together: a 91% report looks like a nearly finished job, and the remaining 9% looks like the to-do list. In the ticketing audit, none of the three real gaps showed up as uncovered lines. The refund module had 80% coverage from a smoke test that asserted nothing.

The tool flags candidates; **you** decide. Also note the checkout e2e test: slowest and flaky, but the only test of the top flow, so it's fixed, not deleted.

Judging a suite only by the code it happens to execute is `mc-high-coverage-well-tested`; untested code is exactly where an audit must look.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: "Fixing" the redundancy test by never flagging anything ("deleting tests is dangerous") is `mc-deleting-tests-risky`. The report surfaces candidates; the judgment happens afterwards, as in the audit worked example.

Finish the project on **your project app**, then summarise here.

1. **Critical flows (obj 3.1):** from your Section 1 risk map, choose one or two flows using the three conditions; write stable e2e tests (Playwright or Cypress) with their own data, role/label selectors and condition-based waits. Run each 50 times in parallel and record failures.

3. **Audit a provided suite (obj 3.3):** run coverage, a mutation tool, and collect runtimes and rerun results; report at least three gaps and three over-investments, each with evidence (a number or mutant id) and an action.
4. **Audit your own suite (obj 3.4):** apply the four lenses, make at least one change (delete, trim, move down a layer, or add a missing test), and record before/after numbers.
5. **Rationale (obj 3.5):** one page or less: context, layers, deliberately untested (with reasons and accepted risk), revisit triggers.

In the box, paste your rationale's *deliberately untested* section and your before/after audit numbers.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Done criteria: every high-risk behaviour on your risk map has a test at a justified layer **or** a reasoned entry under *deliberately untested*; no e2e test failed in the 50-run check; each untested item has a reason, an accepted risk and a concrete trigger; your audit findings each cite a number or mutant id. Final deliverables: all four test layers, risk map, dependency table, `audit-provided.md`, `audit-self.md`, and `TESTING-STRATEGY.md`.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Because value is measured against risk, not runtime alone. The checkout test is the only check that the top revenue flow works as a whole, so its flakiness is a bug to fix. The price-on-page test catches nothing a 4 ms unit test doesn't, and the checkout flow already renders a price, so its cost buys no signal.

workedExamples.title: Auditing the ticketing suite
workedExamples.problem: The ticketing suite has 91% line coverage. Using the audit profile above (runtime, reruns, mutants killed), find at least three over-investments and three gaps.
steps: **Compute the profile** (the runnable block above): total 18,389 ms; slowest and flaky: *e2e: checkout happy path*; redundancy candidates: *api: price endpoint*, *e2e: price shown on page*, *unit: renders logo*.

**Judge each flag.** *renders logo* kills nothing, so delete it. *price shown on page* spends 8.8 s to catch M1, which a 4 ms unit test already catches, and the checkout flow already renders a price, so delete it. *api: price endpoint* is flagged only because the mutants model pricing; it also checks serialisation and routing, so keep it but trim its duplicate pricing assertions.
**Don't obey the tool blindly.** *checkout happy path* is slowest and flaky, but it's the only test of the most important flow. **Fix its flakiness** (worked example s3-we-2); don't delete it.

**Look for gaps against the risk map.** Gap 1: concurrent holds on one seat (nothing tests them; this was the real bug). Gap 2: hold expiry at exactly 10 minutes (covered by the e2e test but never checked at the boundary). Gap 3: refunds on cancelled shows (80% line coverage from a smoke test that asserts nothing).
workedExamples.conclusion: Three over-investments (logo test, price-on-page e2e, the API test's duplicate pricing assertions) and three gaps (concurrent holds, expiry boundary, refunds). **None of the gaps appears as uncovered lines.** Deleting waste, fixing the flaky critical test and adding three small tests makes the suite faster *and* safer.

contentBlocks.content:
## Take it outside the course

An audit is only useful if a team acts on it. Presenting numbers to the people who wrote the tests is where the unstated strategy surfaces, usually in the finding that gets the most pushback.

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Run a two-week test-suite health review on a real codebase, present findings to the team, and propose a written strategy.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: Your workplace, or an open-source project you contribute to
instructions: Collect two weeks of CI data: runtime per test or file, and tests that failed then passed on retry with no code change.

glossary.definition: How much of the system a test runs at once: unit, integration, contract or end-to-end.
A test of one piece of behaviour, in memory, in milliseconds, through a public entry point.
A test that runs your code with real infrastructure such as a database engine, real SQL, the real schema and real serialisation.
A test that checks that separately deployed parts (usually a frontend and a backend) agree on the shape of the messages between them.
A test that drives the whole deployed system as a user would, usually through a browser.
The observation that lower layers are cheaper, faster and better at pinpointing failures, so most tests usually belong low down. A result of trade-offs, not a quota.
Likelihood that something breaks × cost when it does.
A list of an app's behaviours scored by likelihood and impact, with where the logic lives and the layer chosen for each.
A copy of your code with one small deliberate bug, such as `<=` changed to `<`.
Running your tests against many mutants; a failing test **kills** a mutant, and a mutant that passes every test **survived**.
A mutant whose change can't alter behaviour for any input, so no test can kill it.
The percentage of non-equivalent mutants your tests detect (killed or timed out).
A group of inputs that should all behave the same; test the edges of each class.
Anything that stands in for a real dependency in a test.
A test double that returns canned answers.
A test double that is a small working implementation, such as an in-memory outbox.
A test double that records how it was called, so the test can assert on those calls.
A place where a dependency can be swapped without editing the code under test, typically by passing it in as a parameter.
Each test starts from a known state and leaves nothing behind for the next test.
A genuine database engine in tests, rather than a dictionary pretending to be one.
The side that uses an API, such as a frontend.
The side that serves an API.
A contract written by the consumer listing only the requests it sends and the fields and types it relies on, verified by the provider in its own build.
The provider's build running its real handler and checking responses against every consumer contract.
The two sides' idea of a message's shape slowly diverging, e.g. through a renamed or retyped field.
A user journey whose failure costs the most and that depends on many parts working together.
